summary: This memo is an updated policy statement on the schedule for implementing the Domain Style Naming System. It updates RFC 881 and RFC 897 and is an official statement of the IAB and DARPA, pointing elsewhere for how the system itself works.

plainLanguage.summary: A newer calendar for switching everyone to the new names, with the dates changed from before.

subtitle: A dated plan for moving the Internet from one flat host table to hierarchical domain names and name servers.

tldr.problem: The 1983 and early 1984 schedules for adopting domain style names had slipped, and hosts still depended on one centrally maintained table of flat names.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the current, future and transition situations, then sets new dated milestones from 15 Dec 84 to 15 Oct 85 and reviews what happened to the previous schedule.
tldr.outcome: It is an official policy statement of the IAB and DARPA that updates RFC 897 and RFC 881. It is a schedule, not a protocol, so the working details live in other RFCs.

today: RFC 921 updates RFC 897 and RFC 881, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its dates are from 1984 and 1985, and the memo points to RFC 882 and RFC 883 for how the system works.

sections.title: The Current Situation
sections.content:
RFC 921 is a policy statement of the IAB and the DARPA on implementing the Domain Style Naming System. It covers three aspects: the names, the way names are translated to addresses, and the relationship between the Internet and the rest of the world.

Until recently hosts had simple names in one flat space. A name had to start with a letter, end with a letter or digit, use only letters, digits or hyphens inside, and case did not matter, for example USC-ISIF. Hierarchical names have a few components separated by periods, written from most specific on the left to most general on the right, for example USC-ISIF.ARPA. So far every name has the form old-simple-name.ARPA, and the ARPA domain is meant to go away.

Name-to-address translation is done with a table of all hosts, called HOSTS.TXT, maintained centrally at the Network Information Center (NIC). Mail to other systems hides their addresses in the local part and uses a mail-relay host, as in EDMISTON.CIC@CSNET-RELAY.ARPA.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now every computer has a one-word nickname, and one big phone book at one office lists them all. People want longer, organized names and many small phone books instead.

sections.title: The Planned Design and the Transition
sections.content:
The memo expects names to grow in three levels. First, domain style names simply replace old names, with two components, and still translate through the NIC table. Second, names gain more components and more top-level domains, such as F.ISI.USC.EDU. Third, names may identify only organizations, for example USC-ISI.EDU. Mail for such a name needs a lookup, because the server returns a real host that handles mail for the organization, in the example F.ISI.USC.EDU = 10.2.0.52.

Name-to-address lookup is to be done by a number of servers that each hold part of the data, with the database maintained in a distributed way. The design is in RFC 882 and RFC 883. Mail to other systems is also to go through representative organizations listed in the domain servers, as in Oberst@EDUCOM.MAILNET.

The memo stresses that two changes are being made at once: from a full central table to distributed servers, and from flat names to hierarchical ones. The transition plan has two steps, change to domain style names, then change from central tables to name servers. The DARPA research community makes the full transition. The DDN operational community changes names on the same schedule but need not use servers yet; the DDN PMO will set its own schedule later.
sections.plainLanguage: First everyone gets longer, tidier names. Later, instead of one phone book, you ask a helper who knows which small book to check.

sections.title: What Changing Names Costs
sections.content:
All hosts must change their names at least once, and hosts that move to new domains may change several times. A host has an official or primary name and possibly several nicknames, and the official name goes into mail headers.

The memo explains why renaming hurts. Mail sent before a rename cannot be answered with automatic return addresses, Cc addresses are hard to correct, and mailing lists keep stale entries. Its example is a host renamed from FOO to BAR. The general fix is to keep the old name as a nickname for a period, so both old and new names are allowed for a while.

One property must be kept: given any name for a host you can find its address, and given the address you must be able to find the primary name. That calls for careful management of the distributed database by those in charge of the domains and zones.
sections.plainLanguage: If you change your name, old letters addressed to you get lost. So for a while you answer to both your old name and your new name.

sections.title: The Revised Time Table
sections.content:
The memo names three phases: putting machinery in place (servers and resolvers), installing the database, and changing user programs such as mailers. The machinery is well along, with a server for TOPS-20 and two for Unix. The database holds the ARPA domain, and little has been done on user programs. Already done: the protocol and database specification (RFC 882, RFC 883), the domain requirements (RFC 920), domain style names as primary names in the table, and servers for the ARPA domain.

The new milestones are:

  • 15 Dec 84: master table of top level domains and servers at the NIC.
  • 15 Jan 85: new domains may begin to register under RFC 920.
  • 15 Feb 85: principal servers running, and resolvers tested for Unix 4.2bsd and TOPS-20.
  • 15 May 85: programs such as mailers, Telnet and FTP begin regular use of resolvers and servers.
  • 15 Jul 85: the switch to domain style names and servers is to be complete.
  • 15 Sep 85: the NIC host table need no longer be complete for the DARPA research community.
  • 15 Oct 85: the DDN PMO may establish a plan for name service in the DDN community.

An appendix repeats the earlier time table from RFC 897 with notes on what was done, for example the domain style host table was done on schedule while the domain table, multilevel domains and organizational domains were not yet done.
sections.plainLanguage: The calendar lists each step and the date it should be finished, from getting helpers set up to finally retiring the big phone book.

events.label: 15 Dec: master table of top level domains at the NIC
15 May: significant use of resolvers and servers
15 Sep: host table decommissioned for DARPA community
15 Oct: DDN plan for name service
